albums.take: Thirteen years stuck on one song and the album around it is half great. Hell and Back still sounds like a fight I won, Say Please ambushes you at track 11, the middle blurs. Album is worth a shot.
albums.review:
Discover Weekly handed me back a song I had not thought about in years, and about four seconds in I was 23 again.

I was wrapping up college and had just come out of a year of straight F's. My medical leave was not approved, I did not withdraw in time, and the transcript said what it said. I was devastated and I was angry. Then Hell and Back came on.

The song made me feel heard. I had been to hell and back and I was still standing: about to graduate, a year of astronomy research behind me, just home from an observing trip to Lick Observatory. Family matters had cost me a lot and I had thrived anyway. I would put that song on at SW Rec and lift heavy ass weights.

Then I did what you do with a song like that. I played it into the ground and never touched the album around it.

The first twenty minutes are bangers. The title track plays like a movie about teenage heartbreak, and the lyrics are not complicated or deep, but I am not sure they should be for that kind of love. The ending is exactly as soft as it needs to be.

The other surprise came late. Say Please is track 11, almost the last thing on the record, and I fell for those almost haunting chords immediately, and for the cry of "ooooo, oh oh". I had it on at the gym all day today.

The rest does not hold up the same way. Too many songs blur into each other, and an hour later I could not tell you which was which. On the front half alone this is a 4. Whole, a strong 3.5 is fair.
